If ever there was an occasion where the necessity was urgent, and where it had been impossible to foresee the emergency, it was the one alluded to by my right hon. friend. May I quote to him what I urged upon him repeatedly with respect to the use of governor general's warrants? I quote from the Hansard of 1933, March 3, page 2679. Speaking of the use of governor general's warrants to meet emergency relief purposes, I said:
In dealing with questions of great emergency especially where human life is at stake, this House of Commons of Canada has never taken exception to a ministry taking the one course which it can constitutionally take in cases where an appropriation has not been made or is inadequate, of asking for a governor general's warrant to meet a particularly emergent situation until parliament can be brought together. I made it very clear at the beginning of the special session in 1930, that, if the ministry found difficulty in estimating what would be required for the purpose of meeting some very critical situation in the matter of relief, and, if it should be necessary, before parliament could be brought together, that a certain expenditure should be made by governor general's warrants on account of the urgency of the human need involved, those of us who sit on this side of the house would take no exception to that particular course, provided that, in the * first instance, parliament had been given the control it should have.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I have effectively answered my right hon. friend as to the use of governor general's warrants in the case to which he has referred.
In the course of his remarks the leader of the opposition referred to the League of Nations, and with what my rigfht hon, friend said in that connection, as indeed with much else of what he said to-day, I an>
in entire accord. I agree with my right hon. friend when he says that Canada would not have entered the League of Nations had- she not believed that the league was likely to be universal in its membership, and in particular had she not believed that the United States would also be a member of the league.
I shall not at the moment attempt to discuss League of Nations' matters. I may say that at an early stage of the session opportunity will be afforded for the discussion of international affairs when we are taking up the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. However, I should like to reiterate in further part what the right hon. leader of the opposition 'hats said. Because there

has been a failure on the part of the league with respect to some matters for which it was formed, that is no reason why every effort should not be made by the different countries to remedy what defects there may be in the constitution of the league and to change the application of the covenant in such ways as may be necessary to bring about the universality of membership upon which the league was originally intended to be based and without which it is very doubtful if it can be made the success which the nations hoped it would be.
I do not know that there is anything further that need be said in reply bo my right hon. friend, except perhaps a word on the subject of relief. It is quite true that unfortunately the numbers on relief are not diminishing as rapidly as they should. In all countries it has been found that the numbers on relief lag considerably; that they do not show the improvement which it might be expected they would show due to a betterment of conditions as discoverable in increased employment or lessening of unemployment. I think in this country we may take considerable satisfaction out of the fact that the numbers of unemployed are considerably less than they have been and that the numbers employed are greater than for many years. This being so and with recovery taking the strides it is at the present time, it is reasonable to expect that the numbers on relief will rapidly diminish.
The numbers on relief have become what they are largely because of the length of time for which many people held out before taking relief. May I say to my right hon. friend that if at the beginning of his administration he had appointed a commission to take charge of the whole question of relief instead of seeking to have the matter taken care of by a single minister of the crown, with the assistance of his colleagues, I believe that the whole unemployment problem would be vastly different from what it is at the present time. May I say to him further that if under the guise of assistance to the unemployed he had not spent .money recklessly right and left, as he did, for all kinds of purposes we would not to-day have the problem of vast expenditures to deal with which we have. I might add that time is required to offset the ill-effects of wrong policies, and to give right policies a chance to disclose results.
The truth of the matter is that for some years past a great many people have been kept employed not in private enterprise, or in ways which relate themselves to the general business and industry of the country but by public money

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
spent by the government for all kinds of purposes whether profitable or not. When wasteful expenditures are no longer being made, naturally the number of those on relief who have profited by them come to be somewhat larger than they otherwise would be. We have, however, every reason to hope that under the direction of the national employment commission, which has been giving its expert study and guidance to this question, combined with the measures which have been introduced already and which will be introduced later on by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), this most serious problem with which the country has been faced for so many years will rapidly disappear.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to express to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) our great satisfaction at seeing him back in the house. I should like to express also our appreciation of the fine addresses of the mover (Mr. MeLarty) and the seconder (Mr. Veniot) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should like to commend the composers of the speech from the throne. There are in it two things that appeal particularly to us. First, there is the provision for the payment of pensions to the blind. That is highly commendable and very much to the credit of the administration. Second, one passage in the speech reads:
A measure will also be submitted with respect to the discharge, in any coin or currency which is legal tender, of debt payments at present required to be made in gold or gold coin.
The leader of the opposition has pointed out a possible danger in that passage, but it seems to me that it is a step in t'he right direction. I feel encouraged because of it.
Without the desire to criticize in any way,
I should like to take a little time in discussing the question of unemployment and relief. This problem has been brought out clearly by all the speakers who have preceded me. It is a grave problem, but nobody seems to know just exactly what is the cause and nobody seems to be able to give a cure. It seems to me that instead of bandying recriminations back and forth across the floor of the house, we should all get together as a group of earnest and interested members of parliament to see if by pooling our wisdom knowledge and ideas we cannot arrive at a solution of this problem.
I repeat that I am not criticizing the government as I think they have done exceedingly well, all things being considered. Yet I believe it would prove interesting to hon.
members if some excerpts from a report which was made recently were brought to their attention. I have before me a pamphlet entitled The Relief Outlook in Canada, Winter 1936-37, issued by the Canadian Welfare Council on December 28, 1936. This report contains certain passages which certainly are not very comforting reading. For example, at the bottom of page four, I find these words:
As it is, quite apart from drought relief, the loads look as though they would stand (as at the first of December) at a figure representing six per cent to eight per cent increase over comparable 1935 totals.
I assume that this is an official statement of the relief situation in Canada. Again, on page five, we find these words:
With the business index in Canada showing an improvement of more than fifty per cent from 1933; and with employment up about thirty per cent, there can be only grave realization that we are not breaking the line of national relief totals when these show only about eighteen per cent to twenty per cent reduction over those at the corresponding period in the depth of the depression.
I believe that .there is a cause for this relief situation which has not been touched upon so far. There are plenty of people in this house, and plenty of people in this country, who are inclined to scoff at those who undertake to point out that there has been passing over the world during the last decade or so, probably during the last twenty-five years, a great change which has developed largely because of the coming in of the machine and a consequent actual decrease in the amount of wages and salaries and dividends which are going into the hands of the consumers. The consequence is that there actually is being produced among the people, though not among the rich men, of course, or among the bankers, an actual shortage of purchasing power, with the result that it is becoming increasingly difficult to put people to work at profitable labour. This condition is destined apparently to increase in its severity and to bring about more and more unsatisfactory conditions requiring more and more artificial treatment until some fundamental change is made in the way of dealing with social problems in the modem world. Knowing full well that there are plenty of people prepared to criticize, yet I humbly and earnestly submit for the consideration of this house that here is a problem which must be met and solved and which will not be solved by anything which has thus far been presented as a solution of the difficulty.

amount of money, and he said: " That money they are asking for is Canadian money. We Canadian taxpayers have paid that money and that province has no right to come and get it." It would be good for the intellectual development of that writer to take particular notice of the figures which I am about to give to the house. These figures I have taken from some findings which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) made when he was engaged in an investigation in eastern Canada. They are only estimates, but I believe that they are sufficiently accurate for our enlightenment. He finds that, in the incidence of the tariff in Canada, the increase in prices which the people of Manitoba were paying in the year ended March 31, 1931-increases as a result of the tariff-amounted to $29,185,740. The benefit to the producers of Manitoba as a result of those tariffs was only $19,910,971. The loss, then, to the people of Manitoba; in other words, the money which the people of Manitoba contributed to the dominion over and above the benefit they received was $9,274,769. Saskatchewan is faced with a still more serious problem. Her price increase owing to the tariff was $29,228,285 and the only benefit she derived was $3,275,850. The result is that Saskatchewan, in the year ended March 31, 1931, contributed to the dominion treasury, over and above what she obtained as a benefit from the tariff, $25,952,335. How many years that had been going on, and how many years since then a similar drain has existed, is a question which all hon. members must consider seriously. Alberta's price increase was $27,909,396. The benefit to her producers was $8,211,148. The result is that Alberta contributed to the funds of the dominion, over and above the benefit she gained, $19,698,248 in that year, and she has continued to contribute similar amounts since that time. When it can be shown that Alberta has received in return something comparable to that amount, then people will be in a position to talk against Alberta's request for the assistance she needs in a dire way at the present time.
Now let us come to the people of Quebec and Ontario. And before I quote the figures with respect to these two provinces I wish to assure hon. members that I have no desire whatsoever to say anything that would create ill-feeling between the east and the west. We admire and love the east; we are interested in the east and have no wish to cause disunion. But when injustice is borne by any section of the country and continues throughout a long period of years, and when the people who are profiting from that injustice are apparently unaware of its existence and in fact talk in such a way as to be altogether offensive, then

it is high time that those who are being offensive should be informed and should begin to hold their peace. The price increase, so far as Quebec is concerned, was $101,171,562. The benefit to Quebec producers was $132,867,447. In other words, where the three other provinces lost huge sums of money, the people of Quebec, as a result of the tariff, gained the sum of $31,685,885. Now Quebec really ought, under those circumstances, to be able to take care of its relief problems a little better.	[DOT]
Ontario during the same period had a price increase of $168,732,723, but she gained as profit from the tariff, $220,722,484. In other words the gain which Ontario had as a result of the tariff was $51,989,761. Now, when people in two provinces have been benefited to that extent, it thoroughly behooves them to be very careful what they say regarding their suffering neighbours out in the west who have not been by any means so fortunate. So much for the tariff increase.
(Now there is another injustice of which I believe a good many people are not aware.
I am going to speak for a minute or two directly for my own province, not mentioning the others. There is in the Dominion of Canada a freight rate structure that makes Alberta pay both going and coming. She is being discriminated against as is no other province in this dominion. | That ought to be taken into consideration. There are plenty of people who sneer about the Progressive government which the people of Alberta have put into power. I wager that if the people of some of these eastern provinces were suffering as much as Alberta is they would not be as calm as Alberta has been. The thing we want to do is to find what is the cause of all this, and to remove that cause as far as is humanly possible. Surely there is something that can be done. I read this from an editorial in a western paper, and not a Social Credit paper:
This province (Alberta) as a matter of fact is at the apex of the general freight rate struc ture of Canada.
I have not time to go into details, but they bear tremendously on the relief problem in those provinces. Someone is suffering for all that. And it does not matter how desirous they are of working or how careful they are in their living or how economical they are or how anxious to keep off relief, they are in the grip of circumstances which are an absolute disgrace to this dominion.
There are some other things which I wish to consider. I will not now spend any more time on the discrimination; I may at another

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
time say something further on that for the enlightenment of the house. I fancy the reason these things are tolerated is only that we do not know about them. I did not know about these things until I looked them up, and I cannot blame people who have never had them brought to their attention. It is our business to bring them to the attention of hon. members, and we do so in a spirit of good fellowship and straightforward honesty, asking that redress be given to us so that we may live. That is all. You see why I said a moment ago that the matter is exceedingly serious. ) It is positively appalling to the three prairie provinces to have anything said regarding a decrease in their relief appropriation. We are going to recover much more slowly than the other provinces, largely because of the terrible drain that is upon us. But to decrease the appropriation for relief for Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan in proportion to the decrease for Ontario and Quebec, judging from the figures I have brought forward, is to visit upon the three prairie provinces the most shameful discrimination. There should be a greater relief apportionment for those three provinces because of the additional burden that they have to carry. I submit that in all earnestness, and with a desire to cooperate, not in any spirit of criticism or complaining or fault-finding, because that is not the attitude which we in Alberta or we western people take. We come of sires who were pioneers, and pioneers do not come around seeking hand-outs. All we want is something like a decent chance to carry on, and we will carry on.
Now the question may be raised, and I fancy I hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) saying to himself: Yes, but where is the money coming from? Now, I have nothing but the deepest sympathy for any administration which is in power in this country. They face a trying task, one which requires the best judgment that the whole people of Canada can bring to bear upon the situation. There are more reasons than one why that is the case. It may be very difficult under the present structure to see how the money is to be found. I am going to make a suggestion which I know will be received with scorn in many places, but I am going to keep on making this suggestion over and over again, and I say to hon. members:	If I can quote to you great
authorities on. economics, men who should know what they are talking about, and can show that these men favour the ideas which
I bring before this house, then I submit that you would be unwise if you did not give close attention to these ideas.
I am going to suggest that the Dominion of Canada has the authority, according to the British North America Act, to create new money. There are many people who will at once say:	Oh, that will cause inflation.
Now it may be that it will not cause inflation. It is certain that the money can be got in that way, without either taxation or borrowing, and if it is possible so to get money and so to help us to solve our problems, then it is the bounden duty of every hon. member to give that proposal the most careful consideration. In closing my remarks I should like to read to the house a statement from a book by Professor Irving Fisher, professor of economics at Yale university. This book was published in 1935. Its title is "100% Money." Now, I would say that, the considered opinions of a man like that, are worthy of the attention of any man in this house. This man contends that state money is sound money. On page 175 of his book I read these words:
A 100 per cent system using papeT money or credit of the currency commission would be just as effective as a 100 per cent system using gold, as well as less troublesome and clumsy; for, as stated, convertibility into bearer money is the sort of convertibility which is wanted in our modern world-not convertibility into gold ornaments.
It is not at all difficult to see the stand that man has taken, and any man who wishes to consider this matter with great, care and earnestness and honesty will find it greatly to his advantage to read "100% Money" carefully. It shows that I am not altogether crazy when I submit that state money is a feasible suggestion, which ought, to be considered.
At page 188 I find this:
The currency commission should be independent like the supreme court so that the purchasing power of our dollar may be kept stable despite banking operations.
There are many people who say: Oh, we will not put the money into the hands of politicians. Fisher shows the way around. that objection. He says: Just as you have the administration of justice in this land in the bands of men who are independent of politics, so you can put your money affairs into the hands of a group of men who are independent of politics and are held responsible for the efficiency and honesty with which they administer the monetary concerns of the nation. I suggest, then, as a possible way out of the difficulty we have in the

77ie Address-Mr. Blackmore
matter of getting money, that we consider earnestly the question of issuing state money and defraying some of our expenses with that.	_
The matter must be handled with wisdom. Tor those people who say that such money will cause inflation let me use an illustration. When you are in a dry area the first and all important thing is to get water. Having plenty of water someone who does not know how to use it will pour too much water on the land, flood the land and kill the crops or wash them out. The skilled irrigator does not do that. He takes the water and uses it as it should be used, in a scientific manner. The reason we have such fear of inflation as soon as the government begins to deal with money is that we are afraid the government will not be wise in its use of this money when it gets it. Why should that be? If we can learn how to handle everything else scientifically, why can we not learn how to handle our money scientifically? There is no reason at all why inflation should result any more than water flowing down an irrigation ditch should cause a flood.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take up any more of the time of the house to-night. I have outlined in a measure the seriousness of the relief situation, and I very much fear that we are not going to find a solution of this problem until we learn some way or another of financing consumption, of getting money and distributing it among those who are unable to get jobs. I hope we may be able to put all men at work; I rather fancy that if we manage things just right we may be able to do so, but certainly we are not likely to bring about that result by the means we are using at the present time. We may increase our trade as much as we like, but if many men cannot get jobs we are not helping them very much.
Having considered the seriousness of the relief question and having offered what we are ready to present as a solution, I commend this proposal to the serious consideration of this house.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. N. A. MCLARTY AND SECONDED BY MR. C. J. VENIOT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the others who have spoken in complimenting the mover (Mr. McLarty) and the seconder (Mr. Veniot) of the address. I regret, however, that the seconder, in his maiden speech, took occasion to criticise-unfairly, I think- those unfortunate people who are unemployed and on relief. If the conditions which he alleges exist among them actually do exist, then let us face the fact squarely that after six or seven years of unemployment a man

who has reached the age of forty-five or fifty has become unfitted to work again. If the abuses to which the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) referred this afternoon do exist, then I am going to submit on behalf of those people that we must accept some responsibility for that condition. However, undoubtedly we shall have other opportunities to discuss the problem of unemployment, and we can go into this question at that time.
For a moment I should like to turn to the speech from the throne itself. I must say that I do not see in the legislative programme foreshadowed by the speech very much which offers hope to the Canadian people. I am glad, however, that the government is going to bring down for the consideration of this house suggestions in relation to the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. Whatever the outcome, I think that discussion will serve a very good purpose. I am also glad to note that pensions for the blind at a lower age than seventy years are to be introduced. Of course I do not know at what age those pensions will commence, but for my part I should like to see them graduated at least according to physical disability, right from the earliest age until death. I believe that the blind child should be given more assistance bv the state than ordinarily can be given through our regular educational channels; indeed I think some consideration should be given to both the sustenance and the education of the blind child.
Much satisfaction has been expressed already, and I have no doubt more satisfaction will be expressed in the course of the next day or so, by speakers on the government side of the house in regard to the improvement in the economic situation in the Dominion of Canada. There are those, of course, who attribute this improvement to a change of government, when I believe deeper thought would show them that such is hardly the case. No doubt the trade agreement with the United States of America and commerical agreements with other nations have been steps in the right direction, since they make for greater freedom of exchange as between nations. Unfortunately, however, increases in Canada's commercial returns are symptomatic rather of international disease than of international health.
There are two main factors which have contributed to the so-called improved condition. First, there was the impetus given to war preparedness by increasing unfriendliness between the nations of the world and the terrible civil war in Spain. In the second place, as far as we in Canada are concerned,

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
there has been the influence of the short crops of cereals over wide areas of the earth, creating a demand for wheat, which became a commodity asset of tremendous importance in Canada's economic structure. Almost overnight, one might say, our accumulated carryover, of which we heard so much during the last session of parliament, became an asset of vital importance to the world instead of the depressing factor which a more or less crazy economic system made it in the years when it was being accumulated.
The tragedy of the situation at the present time is this, that neither the farmers who produced the wheat nor the Canadian people who carried it through the depths of the agricultural depression have received the maximum benefit to which they were properly entitled. For this, obscured though it be at the moment by rising prices, the selling policy of the present government is in no small measure responsible. Defence of that policy is being made throughout the country and is based upon the assertion that neither the government nor the wheat board could have foreseen the shortage created by the north American drought, and that it was essential to get rid of the accumulated surplus.
When parliament prorogued late in June it was becoming evident that drought was in the making. I motored back to western Canada, and when I passed through North Dakota I saw the crop burning almost hour by hour. When I got back into my own province and my own constituency, in those first days of July, I saw a crop with splendid promise withering visibly before my eyes; yet in that month of July, when it was perfectly evident that, owing to the condition which was developing throughout the whole of the north American wheat belt, wheat must go higher and become an asset of tremendous value, the Canadian Wheat Board sold a record amount of wheat. The amount sold during the month of July, according to the bureau of statistics, reached the enormous figure of 62,302,891 bushels. These sales, might I add, cannot be said to have been made to ultimate consumers. I believe-and my guess in this connection is just as good as that of anybody else

that a great deal of the wheat passed into the hands of various speculative interests, and while we are told that this removed the depressing carryover, it did not in reality remove that carryover .at all. All it did was to change the ownership of the wheat that was carried over; that was .all. Therefore, in view of the situation in North America and the world grain position, [DOT]the setting of the minimum price at 87J cents
a bushel on August 27, with the proviso that the board's operations in relation to the 1936 crop would not begin unless and until the price of wheat fell to 90 cents for No. 1 northern at Fort William, was a distinct disappointment to all our western producers, and I say that knowing that many of the farmers who supported the government which to-day occupies the seats of power in this dominion were just as much disappointed, if not more so, than those who voted against the government.
Subsequent events have shown that the organized farmers of Saskatchewan, in asking for a price of $1.15 a bushel, were not unreasonable. The government and the wheat board together, in my opinion, again deprived the western growers and the people of Canada from reaping the benefit both of the carryover and the world situation. This meant serious losses not only to the farmers but to all those who are dependent on the farmers-the country storekeeper, the doctor, the implement agent, the school teacher, all those whose livelihood depends upon the ability of the farmer to meet his obligations.
Let me remind this house-and I have said this before-that one of the difficulties in western Canada, and indeed perhaps in no small measure the cause of the fundamental economic situation there, is that the farmer, year in and year out, has never received the cost of production of this principal product, wheat. Our university in Saskatchewan states that the average cost over a period of years of producing a bushel of wheat on all types of land in the province is between $1.03 and $1.04 a bushel. If we bear that in mind, it can be readily understood why there was such universal disappointment when the price was set at 87^ cents. This, too, was done on August 27. Now this year we had an unusually early harvest, and a great deal of the crop had already been delivered to the elevators and was in the bins and sold by August 27. Yet, in spite of that, the wheat pools and the western growers endeavoured unsuccessfully to get the government to reconsider its decision.
When at that time the pools asked the government to set the minimum price at one dollar a bushel I do not think they were at all excessive in their requests. By the government's decision providing that delivery would not be taken by the board unless the price of wheat fell to 90 cents, the wheat board was practically eliminated so far as the 1936 crop went, and the western grower was placed very much at the mercy of those great speculative interests which we believe operate in all the

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
grain markets of the world. I submit that existing conditions, in a world of realities, a world of quotas and tariffs and subsidies, demand that we should give our growers protection for their principal commodity, and this is the opinion not only of people who are opposed to the government but of its supporters also.
On April 1 of last year, for example, the Saskatchewan legislature, which is overwhelmingly controlled by friends of hon. gentlemen opposite, adopted a resolution unanimously requesting the continuance of the wheat board and the setting of a minimum price based upon the cost of production. True, a great western paper which is also closely allied with hon. gentlemen opposite stated on August 31 last that no one so far as could be learned was prepared to explain successfully why the cost of production should be the basis of the government fixed price. But surely the serious plight of the western farmer is an ample and sensible explanation of that request. For years he has been disposing of his product at less than the cost of production. If his cost of production is one dollar a bushel and he sella his wheat for 60 cents a bushel, then he has a deficit of 40 cents a bushel, and that deficit must be made up somehow, somewhere, some time. If he has other resources, the deficit is made up from those resources. If he has no other resources, then the deficit is made up by a lower standard of living, by working excessively long hours or from the labour of his wife and family, or from his hired help; finally it is made up out of the equity that he has established in his land, his implements and other resources, and so eventually he passes out. In other words, the deficit represents the exploitation of the producing group by the balance of society. Of course, this sort of policy is a very short-sighted one because the farmer is a part of a great economic machine upon which the manufacturer, the storekeeper, the railroader, the implement company, the banks, the artisans and the labourers all finally depend. Unless all parts of this machine operate smoothly there is disequilibrium in society, a disequilibrium that must lead eventually to social upheaval and to revolution if it is not corrected. Surely that is an entirely sensible reason why at least the cost of production should be the basis of setting a minimum price not only for wheat but for other primary commodities.
If other reasons were needed, all one has to do is to turn to the price spreads investigation or to the recent probe into the textile industry, where the prices have been set, not

directly of course, but indirectly, by tariff protection, for which the farmer and the rest of society must pay. Remove this protection; take over and control these monopolies if you will, and then, perhaps, the costs of production on our farms will drop and standards of living will rise. As long as you compel the farmer to buy in a protected or monopolistic market, you must not be surprised if he in return makes modest demands for protected prices for his products.
To what extent western producers have been exploited by protective tariffs under successive governments, Liberal, Conservative and Union, was shown clearly by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in the figures which have been referred to already and which he presented several years ago before the maritimes commission. May I just repeat some of these figures? He gave the effect of protection for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1931, as an exaction from the three prairie provinces of nearly $56,000,000. The figure for Manitoba was $9,274,000; for Saskatchewan, $25,952,000, and for Alberta, $19,658,000. These were the exactions due to protective tariffs. The cost of the stabilization activities of the late wheat board and the annual cost of relief in the drought areas are a mere bagatelle in comparison.
I would point out to my hon. friends from eastern industrial centres, both Liberal and Conservative, that an elementary sense of justice demands the granting to our farmers of an adequate price for their products. This is surely a sensible reason why -the costs of production should be the basis of fixed prices. Of course, I am not forgetful of the fact that all that has just been said could apply with equal force to other primary commodities. It is sometimes said that we from western Canada are constantly bringing before this house the grievances of the prairie provinces. We are quite aware that the conditions which prevail on the prairies can be duplicated in other parts of Canada. During the recess some of us were able to visit other parts of Canada and we know there is similar distress and there are similar problems among the fruit growers of British Columbia, the farmers and market gardeners of Ontario, the dairymen of Quebec, the fisher folk of the Gaspe peninsula and the maritime coasts, and the workers in industry everywhere. All classes of the community suffer from the same economic conditions which exist to-day in Canada.
We have tremendous distress in the west among our children and our teachers. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I speak for a

The Address- Mr. Coldwell
moment on behalf of these teachers. For twenty-four years I taught in western Canada. I was president of the Canadian Teachers' Federation and I was its secretary for several years. I feel that it is not only a privilege to bring the problems of these people before the house, but more or less an obligation. I am emboldened to do this because of the fact that the teachers of Saskatchewan not very long ago presented a memorial to the government. This memorandum stated quite correctly that the education of its future citizens should be a matter of profound concern to the state. It argued also, again I think correctly, that an enlightened citizenship is the best safeguard of democracy. This memorandum shows how in wide areas of Saskatchewan grasshoppers, drought, soil erosion, frost and depressed conditions generally have made it impossible for local school districts to maintain their educational services as they ought to be maintained.
But for the self-sacrifice of literally hundreds of teachers, schools would have been closed long ago. Their salaries have been reduced again and again. The average reduction in the salaries of rural school teachers in Saskatchewan amounts to sixty per cent. These teachers are receiving only forty per cent of their former schedule. In that province 4,853 teachers signed contracts last year for less than $500 per year. Of that number, 2,419 signed contracts for $400 or less per year. Only a portion of these pitifully small salaries were paid. At the end of 1935, the last record available, the arrears of salaries to the rural teachers of Saskatchewan amounted to over $1,000,000. There are cases of teachers receiving as little as $25 for a term's work. The average net wage in the drought area of Saskatchewan was $10 per month.
Canadian citizens were shocked at the revelations in connection with wages paid by, and working conditions in, certain industries as brought out by the mass buying probe. How much more would Canadian citizens be shocked to realize that persons engaged in a great pulblic service in Saskatchewan are suffering from conditions even worse than those found to exist in certain industries? We heard condemnation this afternoon of those who have allowed these conditions to exist in industry, and yet we have here a great public service where two-thirds of those engaged in it are living below a standard which would not be tolerated even in many of the depressed areas of the world. I have authenticated data showing that teachers have been unable to purchase clothes and that some have been living in cabooses or school basements. The case of a married man with a family was checked up and given to me; I have the name of this man. He has been receiving $20 per month; his groceries, rent and milk cost him $19.50 per month. Not many groceries could be purchased out of that amount. He has fifty cents per month with which to buy clothing and fuel and to pay for health services and so on. There are cases of teachers who are receiving less than $100 for a whole year. Is it any wonder that teachers have been forced to apply for relief while still actively engaged in their work?
This parliament cannot escape all responsibility. I am informed that the interest on the school lands fund, which forms a portion of the revenue of that province, was recently reduced from five per cent to four per cent, thereby reducing the amount available for education. The whole system of organizing and financing education in small semiautonomous and self-supporting units is inadequate and out of date. The time has come to realize that in the interests of democracy and of progress education must be recognized more largely as a matter of fundamental national concern. But apart entirely from these considerations I believe that tb/fc Canadian people would wish this parliament to take steps to ensure that the children in the drought-stricken area of the west shall receive an adequate education under such conditions as will guarantee health and opportunity. Let us remember that present conditions are not going to pass away overnight. One good crop at reasonably good prices will not meet the needs of education and of the agricultural industry to which I have referred. That is why I have been so insistent ever since I have been here that intelligent plans for the rehabilitation of agriculture should form a major task of this house.
Apart from drought problems, to which, I am glad to see, the government is giving some attention, the question of future production and future marketing loom large in the farmer's mind. I know there is a disposition to view with satisfaction the recent rise in wheat prices and there let the matter rest. But in that way future disaster lies. Apart from the fact that under the very best conditions, over a long period, the farmers, the local business men and the public bodies dependent upon both of them cannot liquidate their present debts, there is the question of permanent and remunerative markets to consider. What are the prospects, not in the immediate future, but in the course of the next five or ten years? Has this government any long range policy to place before this

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
parliament? That is a question which should be answered in the affirmative and the policy placed clearly before the house and the country. It is all very well to say that European peoples will compel their governments to lower their tariffs to a point where Canadian, Australian and Argentine farmers will be permitted to market their wheat at adequate prices. There is no real evidence that European governments are going to take steps which would further impoverish their peasant populations. Fear of agrarian uprising to supplement industrial discontent leading to revolution precludes such a possibility. True, during the present crop year certain European nations have imported more than for several years, but only to the extent to which threats of war and short crops impel them to do So. Nor must we forget that in their impoverished condition, aggravated as it has been by the need of raw material, they must restrict their foreign purchases to the extent of their exports.
Like other industrialized and over-capitalized nations, we want to export but to restrict our imports in the interest of a highly protected industrialism. Temporary relief we are enjoying, but it is temporary, and the higher prices in which we are rejoicing are liable to lead us into a new wheat crisis rather than out of a wheat crisis. Higher prices [DOT] will tempt unorganized individual farmers to sow more wheat because they fail to realize that in the exporting countries we have a potential grain producing plant far in excess of the world's present effective consumptive possibilities. The terrible drought of 1936, following as it did several years of other droughts of more or less intensity, obscures this defect in our agricultural position. Canada as a great producer of exportable grain must face the implications of increased productivity of European countries. Who has not noted that in Great Britain they are already considering ways and means of increasing their production of wheat during the coming year? Add to that increased European productivity a declining European birthrate and what is the outlook?
We are told sometimes, of course, that a rising standard of living will solve these problems. But we find this, that up to a certain level large quantities of wheat are consumed; when the standard of living rises above that level the consumption of wheat grows less. More meat is used; more vegetables, more salads, more fruits, more of foods other than basic cereals are used. A few years ago-very recently too-we were told that Japan was a great potential market for 
Canadian grain. Japan is now developing the plains of Manchukuo; and moreover, 'he coming of the soya bean has provided a new food for the eastern peoples. Even in our own country, this great wheat producing land, you can pick up advertisements of bread made with flour derived from the soya bean. Nor must we rely upon the progress of civilization in Asia. Over northern Asia stretches a great nation with vast plains and a highly mechanized agricultural industry; and if new demands come from Asia, Asia in a few years will be able to supply those demands.
Hence the position of Canadian agriculture is a question not wholly of markets, of what we would like, of what we would think, of wider and freer markets-much as I would like to see them in the immediate future- but of intelligent planning to meet the condition which is coming, I believe, after this brief period of higher prices, because the drought condition and consequent grain scarcity will not last forever; we may be quite sure of that.
I know that in saying some of these things I have been running counter to some opinions held by hon. gentlemen opposite. But while I wish to see intelligent, immediate, and quick progress, I do not want to see this country drift towards economic chaos and social upheaval. I want quick progress, but I believe in evolution rather than revolution, and another agricultural crisis, accompanied by the inevitable industrial crisis, would produce a chaotic condition from which we might emerge as some European countries emerged from their crises, with democratic institutions gone, and standards of life greatly lowered. Another crisis such as we have witnessed since 1929 would, I submit, shake our institutions to their foundations and perchance destroy our democracy, at least temporarily. It seems to me that now, when conditions are said to be on the upgrade, we should make preparations to meet the inevitable reaction. That is the opportunity lying before this present parliament of Canada. I wonder if we are going to seize it while there is yet time.
I close with the thought with which I began, that although it may be contended that there has lately been almost phenomenal improvement in certain Canadian industries-and if war comes, those industries may prosper still more-yet, after such a war, we shall suffer more intensely because of the increased production encouraged by war activity. On the other hand war may not come-and I hope that the nations of the world will get together and agree to keep peace and to

The Address-Mr. Fair
disarm-so that the putting into effect of a disarmament program would close many of the markets that we now have. For in relying on potential war industries and prices we are leaning on a broken reed; and as I see it this parliament should lay plans so that we may discover and remove the cause of unemployment, and deal intelligently with agriculture, in order that we may be in a position not only to rehabilitate our farmers in the drought and distressed areas, but to relieve them of their tremendous obligations and burdens of debt, and assist them generally in the days that are to come.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. N. A. MCLARTY AND SECONDED BY MR. C. J. VENIOT
speechtext:
Complying with the suggestion made this afternoon to cut short this session and get through in time for coronation, I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the house on this occasion. I do, however, want bo make a few remarks and at a later date I shall return to the subjects which I am going to touch on at this time.
Since the opening of parliament I have read over the speech from the throne three or four or five times and have been unable so far to get very much out of it. I was glad to learn that trade agreements are being made, but I would suggest that before we export very much of our products the wants of the Canadian people should first be taken care of. That is one of the jobs that we are here to look after.
Following up some of the resolutions brought before parliament at the session a year ago, we find that the government intends to bring down legislation to pay pensions to the blind at an age under seventy years. I am very glad to see that this measure is to be brought in because I believe it is long overdue. However, we believe that it is better late than never and we hope that this legislation will be brought down in the very near future. I also read that there is a marked increase in trade and commerce, accompanied by a noticeable improvement in the general economic situation. I do not know what-particular basic industries this applies to, but I do not believe it applies to agriculture. Perhaps it refers to industries that have fattened at the expense of the agriculturists of the country. I notice also that there has been a pronounced increase in the volume of farm products exported, and that it is the intention of the government to continue the vigorous promotion of the sale of agricultural products at home and abroad. I am not at all surprised at this; I think it very clearly verifies the statement of the head of the wheat
board that that board's job was to get rid of wheat. We must all agree that the board succeeded in getting rid of the grain, but we must also agree that this was done at a terrible cost to the taxpayers of Canada, and particularly those who produced that grain.
Believing that the first duty of a government is to see to the prosperity and happiness of its people, I am now bound to take advantage of this first possible opportunity to condemn the action of the government in getting rid of our wheat board. This legislation was brought down in 1935. Resolutions from several organizations throughout the country have been presented to the government, petitions have been signed by thousands of growers in the west, many boards of trade and several other organizations to keep that marketing board in operation. But we find that the intelligence of the people of Canada has been slammed by this action of the government in disposing of that board. I do not agree that the price of 87i cents set by that board was sufficient, but that was better than nothing, because those who delivered, grain to the wheat board were given certificates by which they collected any profit that was gained at a later date. Now, in spite of these resolutions and petitions to which I have referred, the government has seen fit to drain these profits away from the producers and to throw them into the laps of the gamblers on the Winnipeg grain exchange. I do not think this is good business, and if the matter had been handled by a board of efficient men working in the interests of the producers, who are certainly entitled to have something to say about the sale -of their grain, and working also in the interests of Canada as a whole, I believe that instead of a deficit of something like $11,800,000 there would have been a large sum of money to distribute to the producers who delivered that wheat to the board. Instead of that we have perhaps thirty cents a bushel clear profit turned over to somebody who did not turn a hand in the production of that grain. In my opinion that is not good business, because I believe that the farmers and other people in the west have been sufficiently gypped in the past in connection with wheat. I am referring now to the settlement of the 1930 wheat pool payment. In that case we were gypped 4-2 cents a bushel on the average price of grain in 1930, and I believe that we were gypped as high as fifty per cent of the amount we received from these wheat pool payments, in the amount of interest we paid on debts which should have been paid with the money that was tied up in this wheat and held by both our governments. Five years
The Address-Mr. Fair

after we were entitled to our payment we got it, and, as I said before, at least fifty per cent of that amount was consumed in interest.
Figures have been put out by the dominion government showing that in 1932 the average cost of growing wheat was 95 cents a bushel. That 95 cents does not include approximately 19 cents for freight and handling charges, which would mean a gross payment of $1.14 at Fort William. That, I believe, is based upon an average of approximately sixteen bushels per acre. This year, instead of getting sixteen bushels per acre, there are thousands of farmers who did not get two bushels per acre, and in a good many cases we find that thousands of acres have been left without a binder being brought in. So when the government tells us that we are making profits on this year's grain and that our basic industry is improving, it is a statement that needs to be revised.
I listened last session to one member of the medical profession who sat to my right; this afternoon I listened to another who sat opposite. If his talk had not been so far from the truth I think I might have enjoyed it. I have to take very strong exception to the statement of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) in regard to those on relief and unemployed. The hon. member said this afternoon that if our governing bodies expect to pull out of this morass of unemployment, our only hope lies in getting people back to work-consciousness, compelling them to give some personal return for the assistance they receive, by cutting out this panhandling, this racketeering, this subsidizing of idleness, this sponging on the public treasury on which so many persons have existed dishonestly for the last five or six years. As a representative of the down and out people as well as a few of the other class I take very strong exception to those words "dishonestly for the last five or six years." If that had been directed somewhere else I might not have objected, but in connection with those poor down and out people on the relief roll I must stand up and have that statement withdrawn. If it is proven, then let us get busy and correct it. It is up to someone to remedy that condition. Ninety per cent of those on relief to whom I have talked would work and make a good job of it if only they were given something to do and some remuneration for that work.
We are told that the government is doing quite a lot by putting men on the farms. They are sending men out on the farms at $5 a month. I think it is an insult to the intelligence of Canadians to have in operation a system that will send anybody out at a wage

of $5 a month. If our present system is not capable of giving people a decent living then it is time to change that system, and if those in office cannot tell how to change it they should get out and let others in who will at least see that our people get enough to eat, enough to wear and a decent house to live in.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. N. A. MCLARTY AND SECONDED BY MR. C. J. VENIOT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that it is the desire of the house to take a vote this evening, and I do not intend to delay the vote. I should, however, like to make a few brief remarks relative to the speech from the throne, and I assure the house that if they will bear with me I shall try to be very brief.
Since the last session of this parliament many events of marked importance have taken place both in Canada and abroad. Those outside Canada have been the cause of much concern to us and have made us wonder whether another great conflict was not in course of preparation. In Europe the political atmosphere is clouded with uncertainty. Recent events in Spain, the verbal dual between Germany and Russia, the ever-increasing exigencies of dictatorship countries, have rendered the situation perplexing and embarrassing, and the consequences at the present time are very grave. The clash, should it come, seems likely to be one between classes, infinitely more serious than that between nations. In the international realm this country has moved with great caution. The attitude adopted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at Geneva, should, I believe, commend itself to the vast majority of the citizens of this country. The action of the several cabinet ministers in seeking to open up trade channels with the great countries of Europe has received nation-wide recognition. The idea of getting away from economic isolation has done much not only in preparing the way for peace but also in preparing the way for recovery toward which we are rapidly progressing.
Internally Canada's position, while still a serious one, and while still faced with major issues, indicates that we are fast emerging from the depression. We cannot but breathe a sigh of relief in scanning the figures of our export trade. With reference to this it is only fair to say that in the relatively short time this government has been in office it has guided the destiny of the nation safely and well. That it may continue to do sc, and may pilot the ship of state safely into port, is the hope of all those who have at heart the interests of their country.
There has been marked recovery in agriculture. The cheese industry particularly has been active. Never since 1930 have cheese

The Address-Mr. Chewier
prices reached the level which they did in 1936, the average yearly price per pound for that year being approximately 13 cents; the exact figure was 12-76. The value of cheese exports for 1936 exceeded the figure for 1935 by over $4,000,000. It is remarkable to note that the greater part of this increase in exports went to the United Kingdom, and the remainder to the United States of America. It is also interesting to note that there was exported to the United States in 1935 only $77,289 worth of cheese, whereas in 1936 there went to that country one and a half million dollars worth. It is also important to note that the total production of cheese in Canada during the twelve months just ended increased by 17-8 per cent. This is only one branch of agriculture, and it is worthy of note that this has been achieved without the intervention of the bonus. The farmer, as hon. members know, has had very difficult times in the recent past and we should be generous to him, because in times of difficulty, in times of economic strain, it is toward the farmer that we look very often for assistance. Therefore, when recovery and its forces are in the offing we should be generous with him.
The expansion in our export trade has been striking, as has been pointed out by one of the speakers this afternoon. The total exports for last year amounted to over $928,000,000. which is an increase of 22-6 per cent over 1935. For the twelve months' period, when the figures are known, they will doubtless be well over the billion dollar mark. The total favourable trade balance for the eleven months amounted to over $346,000,000, and while this is not a record it has been exceeded on only two previous occasions. The trade treaty with the United States is responsible in no small measure for the substantial increase in our export trade.
The national housing policy recommended by the employment commission and adopted by the government has already done much in reducing the number of unemployed. We can look to the future with confidence.
The county of Stormont, which I have the honour of representing in this house, apart from being the most beautiful in this dominion, is typical of the country in which we live. It is partly industrial and partly agricultural. Ethnically it is not unlike many of the great constituencies of this country, because in Stormont there live side by side descendants of the two great civilizations, the English and the French, which have contributed so much toward the development of this country. And
what is more, these people live in perfect harmony. Of this there could be no greater proof than that the constituency, although in the majority English speaking, has seen fit to send to this house as its representative a citizen of French origin. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the English speaking element of my constituency would wish me at this juncture to address myself to the house in the French language.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I simply wish respectfully to salute in my mother tongue, which is also yours, the French-Canadian element- of my constituency. This element is composed mostly of workingmen and farmers, and in thinking of them I am reminded of the words of Longfellow in his immortal Evangeline:
Men whose lives glided on like rivers that water the woodland; darkened by shadows of earth but reflecting an image of Heaven.
Today the working masses are suffering; in nearly every country in the world they are the victims of individualism with its doctrine, its utilitarianism and its unrestricted competition which has degenerated in economic dictatorship, and the people are ready to believe that the only remedy to their evils lies in a complete overthrow of the social order. It is necessary to prove to those who suffer an-dj are embittered against society that the remedy does not reside in the destruction of the existing order, but in its reform, for otherwise it will be impossible effectively to defend society against the assault of revolutionary forces.
If, Mr. Speaker, the forces of recovery are in the ascendant in some phases of the nation's activities, there is one phase in which those forces seem to be entirely lacking. That is in the relationship between capital and labour. The underlying causes of the depression are numerous. There is one, however, which stands out among all the rest, and that is the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a few. There is another outstanding cause, if I may so say; that is, the abnormal relationship which presently obtains between capital and labour. There may be signs of recovery in the offing, but recovery in the true sense must benefit all classes of society, the poor as well as the rich, the feeble as well as the strong, the farmer and the wage earner as well as the high salaried director. In order to have stability in recovery there must be a more equitable distribution of wealth.
With the permission of the house, sir, as briefly as possible I should like to outline what I believe to be the true relationship which should exist between capital and labour and

The Address-Mr. Chewier
which should bring to the working classes of this country a fairer share of the comforts of life to which they are justly entitled. Capital is the money, plant and machinery of the manufacturer, called the capitalist or employer, while labour is the work done or services rendered by the employee for the employer. Both of these great agencies are essential factors in the community, and neither can do much without the other. Both together produce what society needs. Then there is another all important factor, sir, and that is the community itself. Among these three great factors there should exist the closest cooperation and harmony. To some extent, perhaps, there should be a degree of partnership, and the three should work together for the common good.
Unfortunately, however, such is not the case. When industries establish themselves in a community many advantages are held out to them. They are given fixed assessments over a period of years, cheap water power and very often transportation facilities. In return for these advantages industries agree to erect certain plant and machinery and to employ large numbers of men. On their part there is also an implied obligation to employ these men under fair working conditions and to pay them just and equitable wages. There is also an obligation to employ them in such a manner that their health will not be injuriously affected. Many industries, however, have little or no regard for implied obligations. Some of them pay much more attention to their machinery than they do to the men who operate it. The result is that in some communities, instead of having the harmony and cooperation which should exist between the forces of capital and labour, there is a cleavage, and we have two groups each opposing the other, to the great detriment of the community.
The relationship of capital and labour is brought about by means of the contract of labour. The contraot of labour is the leasing or hiring not of a material thing but of the services of an individual, that is, of a human being, and it is impossible to separate the individual from his work. The contract of labour embodies two obligations: first, that of paying for the services rendered according to their value and, second, that of making use of the object leased or hired according to its nature. The contract of labour might be likened to the leasehold of premises. In the leasehold of premises the tenant takes upon himself the obligation not only of paying rent but also of making use of the premises during the currency of the term in a fair and reasonable manner, and of giving up the premises

at the end of the term in the same condition as they were at the beginning, reasonable wear and tear excepted. So in the contract of labour the employer agrees not only to pay a fair and reasonable wage to the employee but abo not to abuse his services, so that when he has completed his work his health will not have been injuriously affected.
Unfortunately, sir, in many instances these obligations on the part of the industries are not respected. In numerous cases men and women are paid wages which are not only unfair and unjust but which are a disgrace to those who pay them. Furthermore, oftentimes men and women are made to work under conditions which are not only injurious to their health but, on account of the speed up and stretch out systems, tax their physical capacity to such an extent that their nervous system thereby becomes affected, and sooner or later they must give up their work and seek employment elsewhere. The reason for this unfair advantage being taken of the working classes is that in our day the manufacturer has become so powerful that he can dictate his terms and conditions to the labourer, who must accept them or very often do without work. Such a condition should not be allowed to exist, and in my humble opinion there should be state intervention.
I should like to go a step further and outline what I understand by a fair and reasonable wage. The general rule, sir, is that the employer should give the employee a wage or salary according to the value of his work, and in order to determine the value of a man's work it is necessary to consider its nature. Why does man work? Is it simply to chase away the blues, to form his character or to develop his muscular strength? To some extent, yes, but it is chiefly and mainly to earn a living. That is the reason man works; that is the object and end of man's work. Employer and employee may, if they so desire, bargain for a fixed wage, but over and above their bargain there stands the law of natural justice, more ancient and more sacred than all other laws, which stipulates that the wage paid by the employer to the employee should be a reasonable wage that will allow the employee to live respectably. This means that the wage should be sufficient to allow him to support and maintatin his family, pay his rent take an honest recreation from time to time and allow him to put something to one side for the day of sickness and difficulties. It is a known fact that wages in some industries are such that it is impossible for a man to maintain his family let alone pay rent and enjoy some of the ordinary comforts of life to which he is justly entitled.

The Address-Mr. Chevrier
During the depression, Mr. Speaker, many corporations pay and are still paying enormous salaries to their directors and hand out huge dividends to their shareholders, but they fail and are still failing to pay to their employees a just and equitable wage. I said a moment ago that I thought there should be state intervention, but I believe that first of all the problem is one which should be settled by the manufacturers because they are primarily responsible. It is they who have created the problem, and they should help to solve it. If they were to give to the solution of this problem but a fraction of the time they devote to their own affairs I believe they could solve it. Unfortunately, however, they seem to be concerned only in what will help them to advance their own interests, and when the state is asked to intervene, and says that it will intervene, the manufacturers object strenuously on the ground that there must be free and open competition, and on the further ground that wages must be fixed according to the law of supply and demand. They maintain the right to give the employee the wage which they can get him to accept. On the other hand they maintain the right to form huge monopolies, such as those of coal, gasoline, milk, meats, bread and other commodities, and when once these are established they sell to the consumer at the highest possible prices. They want the right to amass huge fortunes and still pay ridiculously low wages. If the employees threaten to organize, the manufacturers object, and yet they belong to the strongest price organizations of the world.
The time has come, to my mind, when there should be state intervention. There should be legislation governing the hours of work in each day and the days of work in each week. There should be minimum wage laws for men. There should be legislation governing the conditions under which men and women have to work. True, these are all matters outside the jurisdiction of this house unless, of course, the privy council should otherwise decree, but this house holds in its hand a powerful weapon with which it might strike, and that is the tariff. Many industries are in need of a protective tariff. There are some which could not carry on without it. I believe that every legitimate industry should be protected, but upon the distinct understanding that it will pass on to its employees in the way of better wages and better working conditions the benefits of this tariff so ardently sought.
At the turn of the century, Mr. Speaker, economic conditions in industry had a tendency in practically every nation to divide society into two groups; on the one hand,
a minority of rich people holding power and wealth in their hands and enjoying all the benefits which modem invention could offer; on the other hand, a vast majority of working people enduring great hardships and attempting to extricate themselves from this condition as best they could. By the minority this condition was accepted as the result of the economic laws and as a condition which had always existed to a certain degree. The majority, however, refused to submit themselves to this condition, which was intolerable, and many of them thought that the only solution lay in a complete downfall of the social order.
As I sat in this house during the last session, Mr. Speaker, I heard reechoed on many occasions in this chamber the words, "democracy is on trial." There is no greater truism than that statement. But sometimes I wonder what is being done to save democracy. It is being attacked on all sides. It has committed many errors. It has been guilty of many crimes, and it is badly in need of reform. Many theories have been advanced to supplant it, and among them are communism and fascism, but these are remedies worse than the evil. Both are incompatible with the traditions and institutions of this country, and if those theories were to prevail there can be no doubt that complete ohaos would follow in this country.
The solution, in my humble opinion, lies in reform and in a return to those two virtues of justice and charity, virtues as old as the day is long but which with the dawn of a new era see-m to have been relegated to the past. If those institutions which hold in their hands power and wealth were to abandon 'their ideas of individualism and egotism and to mete out more in the way of justice and more in the way of charity, I believe that equilibrium in society would soon be restored. I believe, too, that the forces of capital and labour would take in society the positions they were meant to take, that of cooperating one with the other, of a harmonious relationship, of working together for the common good of all.
There is one other class in society which, I believe, deserves the condemnation of this house, and that is the group of agitators who have been at work within recent months with the object of creating excitement among the working classes, and with the object of confusing the working people for their own subversive ends. To use the words of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in his New Year's eve message to Canada, "I believe that an intelligent public opinion will sooner or later condemn these agitators."
Main Estimates

It must be a source of gratification to this government, Mr. Speaker, to know that the forces of recovery are again in the ascendant. But this time let us have recovery in the true sense of the word; let us have recovery which will benefit all classes of society, from the most humble citizen of the realm to the most powerful. In that way those forces which seek the downfall of the social order will soon disappear, and we in Canada will march on toward higher and better things.
Motion (Mr. McLarty) agreed to.
